prompt: According to the course, in which stage of the industry life cycle are buyers' bargaining power high and the threat of new entrants low?
explanation: Introduction: low rivalry. Growth: low rivalry, low buyer power, high supplier power. Shakeout: high rivalry. Maturity: high buyer power, low threat of entry. Decline: high rivalry.

prompt: Which dimensions are used to define strategic groups? Select all that apply.

options.text: Product range and geographical coverage (scope of activities)
Branding effort, quality and vertical integration (resource commitment)

explanation: Scope: product range, geography, segments, channels. Resource commitment: branding & marketing, vertical integration, quality, R&D, size.

prompt: CitizenM removed restaurants from its hotels. In the ERRC grid this is…
explanation: Eliminate restaurants; reduce room space and reception; raise low-cost construction; create the combination of 5* location/comfort with 3* prices.

prompt: Which statements describe the strategy canvas logic of a blue-ocean player? Select all that apply.

options.text: It maintains adequate performance on the CSFs where rivals compete harshly
It invests in new CSFs that are valued but left unexplored
It tries to outperform every rival on every existing CSF
It stays above the minimal performance level needed to survive

explanation: Company C in the slides keeps adequate (not maximal) performance on cost, after-sale service and quality and focuses on testing services and design advice – new CSFs.

prompt: Which of Nintendo's consoles are presented as moves into a red ocean? Select all that apply.
explanation: 3DS (3D screen of little value, high costs) and Wii U (technically obsolete vs smartphones/tablets) competed on technology. Wii, DS and Switch created new market space.

prompt: “Creating a blue ocean means making our existing customers even happier.” Which of the six traps does this statement fall into, and what is the remedy?

options.text: Trap one – focus on noncustomers instead
Trap six – focus on low costs
Trap four – destroy the existing market

explanation: Trap one: making existing customers happier keeps you in the red ocean. Market-creating strategies look at noncustomers of the industry.

prompt: A strategic group map of hotels shows an empty space for “luxury hotels with very low prices”. What should an analyst ask first?

options.text: Is it a white space (opportunity) or a black hole (dead end, e.g. economically unviable)?
How to enter it as quickly as possible, since empty spaces are always profitable
Which rival has the highest market share

explanation: Unoccupied spaces can be opportunities or deadlocks. Analysts also check mobility barriers to reach them.

prompt: Which lessons does the course draw from the Nintendo case? Select all that apply.

options.text: Customers determine what is valuable, not producers
Technological innovation is neither sufficient nor necessary to unlock new markets
Nintendo performed best when it imitated rivals on technology

explanation: When Nintendo competed via technology (N64, GameCube, 3DS, Wii U) it performed poorly; when it escaped competition (NES, DS, Wii, Switch, Pokémon Go) it performed well.

statement: Competitive dynamics are usually more intense within a strategic group than between groups.
explanation: Firms with similar scope and resource commitments target similar customers on similar dimensions.

statement: Mobility barriers are barriers to entry between strategic groups.
explanation: E.g. a corner shop cannot easily become a supermarket (capital, scale, supplier relations).

statement: A blue ocean strategy must be based on a technological breakthrough.
explanation: Trap three: confusing technology innovation with market creation. The Wii used low technical standards; value innovation matters.

statement: Blue ocean strategies aim to combine differentiation and lower costs.
explanation: Traps five and six: market creation is neither pure differentiation nor pure low cost.

statement: According to Kim & Mauborgne, market-creating strategies segment the market into smaller niches.
explanation: Trap two: niche strategies segment markets; market-creating strategies de-segment them by attracting noncustomers.

statement: In the growth stage of the industry life cycle, suppliers tend to have high bargaining power.
explanation: Demand grows faster than capacity, so inputs are scarce.

statement: Defining an industry too broadly or too narrowly can distort the analysis.
explanation: Choose criteria such as geography, product segment and position in the value chain; watch for converging industries.

statement: WeWork's self-description as a technology platform changed the Five Forces of its industry.
explanation: Calling yourself “tech” does not change the forces: low entry barriers, long fixed leases vs monthly revenue, high rivalry – a blue-ocean trap.

statement: Blue Ocean Strategy reorients strategic thinking from competitors to alternatives and from customers to noncustomers.
explanation: How to make competition irrelevant and create new demand.

prompt: Apply the four actions framework (Eliminate, Reduce, Raise, Create) to Nintendo's Wii.
modelAnswer: Eliminate: the race for graphics power and high-definition processing, complex controllers with many buttons. Reduce: technical specifications and production costs, game complexity and learning costs for new players, price of the console. Raise: fun, social and family play, accessibility for non-gamers (elderly, families). Create: motion control with the Wiimote, physical activity and party games (Wii Sports, Wii Fit). Result: a new market space of casual and family gamers (noncustomers of Sony and Microsoft) with lower costs and high value – value innovation rather than technological competition.
keyPoints: Link to noncustomers and lower costs (value innovation)

prompt: What are strategic groups, how are they identified, and why are they useful for strategic analysis?
modelAnswer: Strategic groups are sets of organizations in an industry that share similar strategic characteristics. They are identified along two types of dimensions: scope of activities (product range, geography, number of segments, distribution channels) and resource commitment (branding and marketing effort, vertical integration, quality, R&D, size) – e.g. supermarkets, convenience stores and corner shops in grocery retail. They are useful because (1) they show with whom a firm actually competes and on which dimensions – rivalry is most intense within groups; (2) they reveal unoccupied spaces that may be white spaces or black holes; (3) they highlight mobility barriers that protect a group and limit moves between groups.
keyPoints: Scope and resource-commitment dimensions with examples
Uses: real competitors, white spaces/black holes, mobility barriers

prompt: Present the six red-ocean traps identified by Kim & Mauborgne.
modelAnswer: 1) Making existing customers happier – instead focus on noncustomers. 2) Treating market-creating strategies as niche strategies – market creation de-segments markets. 3) Confusing technology innovation with market creation – value innovation matters. 4) Equating creative destruction with market creation – new markets need not destroy existing ones. 5) Equating market creation with differentiation – it also requires lower costs and prices. 6) Equating market creation with low-cost strategies – it also requires differentiation.
keyPoints: Not only differentiation / not only low cost
